**David Ricardo**
The British classical economist most commonly credited with this concept. He used it to argue for free trade, and his name is the usual giveaway for the answer.

**On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation**
Ricardo's 1817 treatise, which contains the classic explanation of this concept. Its famous example has England and Portugal trading cloth and wine: Portugal can make both more efficiently, yet both countries gain when each specializes in the good it produces relatively more cheaply.

**Robert Torrens and the Corn Laws**
Robert Torrens described the idea first, in an 1815 essay on the Corn Laws, Britain's tariffs on imported grain. Ricardo's later version became the standard one.

**Opportunity cost**
The value of the next-best alternative given up to produce something. Under this principle, a country should export goods it can produce at a lower opportunity cost than other nations, and import goods that other nations produce at a lower opportunity cost.

**Absolute advantage**
The ability to produce a good with fewer resources than another producer, an idea associated with Adam Smith. Comparative advantage shows that a country gains from trade even if it has no absolute advantage in any good, because what matters is relative cost.

**Specialization**
Comparative advantage explains why countries specialize in producing certain goods. When each country focuses on the goods where its opportunity cost is lowest, total world output rises.

**Production possibility frontier**
A curve showing the combinations of goods an economy can produce with its resources. Specializing and trading by comparative advantage lets countries consume combinations of goods outside their own production possibility frontiers.

**Gains from trade**
The extra goods both partners can consume after specializing and trading. Comparative advantage is the main theoretical argument that free trade benefits all participants, not only the most efficient producer.

**Ricardian model**
The simple trade model built on Ricardo's idea, in which labor is the only factor of production and differences in labor productivity between countries determine what each exports.

**Heckscher-Ohlin model**
A later trade theory that explains comparative advantage through differences in factor endowments: countries export goods that use their abundant factors, such as capital or labor, intensively.
